summary: Long one of the world's hardest countries to visit, Equatorial Guinea still routes most nationalities through its embassies, although the UK FCDO also describes an online e-visa application. US citizens have needed a visa too since April 2023, when their long-standing exemption was cancelled; CEMAC neighbors enter freely.

notes: Photography of the presidential palace, ports, airports, military sites and government buildings is prohibited — cameras and phones can be seized.

payments.text: Cash in CFA francs covers almost everything. Cards are accepted only at the few international hotels in Malabo and Bata, and ATMs are unreliable. Bring euros or US dollars to exchange.

safety.text: Violent crime is comparatively rare, but travelers face frequent police checkpoints, document checks and occasional petty extortion; photography rules are strictly enforced. Carry certified copies of your passport and visa at all times.

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to February is the driest, most comfortable window on Bioko island (Malabo) and pleasant on the mainland; rain falls year-round, peaking around April–May and October.

tips.text: US citizens no longer enter visa-free. Equatorial Guinea cancelled the exemption in April 2023, and the US Embassy in Malabo asks travellers to ignore websites that still say otherwise. Apply for a visa at least 60 days before you travel.

Do not photograph the presidential palace, airports, ports, checkpoints or anything military or governmental. The rules are enforced and cameras or phones can be confiscated; ask permission before photographing people.
Carry your passport (or a certified copy) and visa at all times — police checkpoints are frequent on Bioko and the mainland, and missing documents commonly lead to fines or lengthy delays.

The UK FCDO describes an online e-visa application for what was once one of the world's hardest tourist visas, but Equatorial Guinea's own government publishes no eVisa page we could find: confirm the current application channel with an Equatoguinean embassy before relying on it, and avoid unofficial visa websites.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Equatorial Guinea?
faq.answer: Most nationalities do. The Embassy of Equatorial Guinea in Washington states that every visitor with a foreign passport must present a valid visa at the point of entry; you can apply at an embassy, and the UK FCDO also describes an online e-visa application. That includes US citizens, whose visa-free arrangement was cancelled in April 2023. CEMAC citizens (Cameroon, Chad, CAR, Congo, Gabon) move freely.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Equatorial Guinea?
faq.answer: Yes. Equatorial Guinea cancelled visa-free travel for US passport holders on 24 April 2023, and its Embassy in Washington says every visitor with a foreign passport must present a valid visa. The US Embassy in Malabo advises applying at an Equatoguinean embassy at least 60 days before travel and ignoring websites that still describe the old exemption.

faq.question: Does Equatorial Guinea have an eVisa?
faq.answer: Yes, according to the UK FCDO: complete the online visa application and upload the documents, allow 72 hours for processing, then print the e-visa letter and present it on arrival, where border officials issue the visa. Equatorial Guinea's own government publishes no eVisa page we could find, so confirm the current channel with an Equatoguinean embassy before you rely on it.

faq.question: Is Equatorial Guinea really that hard to visit?
faq.answer: It was long ranked among the world's most difficult destinations — few embassies, demanding paperwork and discretionary refusals. The online e-visa the UK FCDO describes makes applying easier, but expect more documentation than usual (hotel booking, bank statements, sometimes police clearance) and allow plenty of time.

faq.question: Is Equatorial Guinea safe for travelers?
faq.answer: Broadly yes in terms of crime, which is low by regional standards. The friction points are bureaucratic: frequent police checkpoints, strict photography rules and document checks. Keep your papers on you, avoid photographing anything official, and travel patiently.
